doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: How he thinks when improvising
summary: He thinks chordally, embellishing the changes, hearing some notes as if reading them.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: All right. Well said. A little earlier we were kind of joking about the theory behind music and how it’s sometimes overdone and the mode thing and all that. Is it possible for you to describe your thinking process when you improvise, and how much of it is affected by your knowledge or lack of knowledge of chord structure and all that?

Oh it’s affected very much by my knowledge of chord structure and my ear, to be able to hear chord changes. And everything that I do improvisational-wise is — everybody does it differently. Everybody thinks differently. The way I think is chordally by an extension of the chords. For instance, I think, if it’s a G seven chord I may play the ninth or the flatted ninth or the lowered fifth or these kind of things. And move into the next change. I used to know a guy in New York who used to teach an improvisational course and he would teach the kids learning chord changes by thinking they were changing keys. Okay, now for a while if you’ve got a two-five-seven in B flat, you’re in B flat. But now the next chord change is a two-five-seven in G you now change to the key of G, and so forth and so on. It worked for some of them. It never worked for me. Because it confused me. So my approach to it was always what the chord changes are, and working around those changes and embellishing those changes. I mean it may not be written a G nine, but you can play a ninth on top of a G seven, that kind of thing. And that’s basically the way I’ve always approached it. And what goes on in my mind is I see the notes as if I was actually reading them on a page. But up to a certain point. I see some of them. I don’t see all of them.
I like that analogy. Right. Because you can almost hear some of them but not quite all of them.
Exactly. You’ve got to have a couple in the middle before you get to the next one.
To get where that thing is you can hear. Yeah, those are the passing tones, right?
